report.source_text: Since P. micra and C. rectus are both members of the oral flora, a dental origin of infection was considered. The patient reported to not have seen a dentist for more than 10 years, while dental hygiene seemed rather poor. Our patient therefore was referred to the dental department where a chronic periodontitis was diagnosed. Tooth 47 was not vital, and loss of previous cavity occlusion was reported in tooth 36. Remaining dental examination remained unremarkable.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A mid-40s Tanzanian female presented with a 4-week progressive chest wall swelling culminating in spontaneous rupture of a purulent abscess without fever. Physical exam confirmed a large chest wall abscess on the sternum region. CT imaging revealed osteomyelitic erosion of the sternum with a large abscess extending to neck muscles but sparing intrathoracic spaces. The patient had poor dental hygiene and was diagnosed with chronic periodontitis. Cultures from sternal bone and deep tissue grew oral flora bacteria P. micra and C. rectus. No trauma or other infection sources were found, linking oral infection to the primary sternal osteomyelitis and abscess.
